name: Semiaquatic pursuit predator
claim: Spinosaurus spent substantial time in water, possibly swimming after fish, with a paddle tail and dense bones providing propulsion and buoyancy control.
support: Dense limb and axial bones have been interpreted as ballast for subaqueous foraging.
The distal tail has tall neural spines and long chevrons, producing a broad paddle.
The long, narrow snout and conical teeth resemble those of fish-eating crocodilians.
Fish remains occur in the same deposits, and the snout is well suited to capturing slippery prey.
criticism: The skeleton is highly pneumatic; buoyancy may have made habitual diving difficult.
The hind limbs are short and the forelimbs are not obviously adapted for aquatic propulsion.
Bone-density methods and their statistical treatment have been criticised.
A swimming animal would leave a distinctive taphonomic and sedimentological signal that is not clearly established.

name: Shoreline generalist
claim: Spinosaurus was primarily a terrestrial animal that hunted and scavenged along rivers and coastlines, wading in shallow water rather than pursuit-swimming.
support: The skeleton retains features associated with terrestrial weight support.
A pneumatic skeleton would have been buoyant and unstable in deep water.
The long snout could be used to strike at fish from the water’s edge.
The deposits preserve a range of terrestrial and aquatic organisms, not a deep-water assemblage.
criticism: The extremely short hind limbs and long torso are unusual for a purely terrestrial theropod.
The tail paddle is difficult to explain without some aquatic function.
Dense bones are not expected in a fully terrestrial animal.
The ecological role of the animal remains poorly constrained by direct evidence.

name: Quadrupedal or bipedal?
claim: The 2014 reconstruction proposed a quadrupedal animal with a forward-shifted centre of mass. Later work argued for a more conventional bipedal stance.
support: Short hind limbs and a long torso shift the centre of mass forward.
The forelimbs are robust and could, in principle, bear weight.
Quadrupedality is rare among theropods but not impossible.
criticism: The forelimb joints and hand morphology are not obviously adapted for habitual quadrupedal walking.
Trackways that might record Spinosaurus are not confidently associated with the animal.
The centre-of-mass reconstruction depends on the soft-tissue model used.
